title: Cosmic 'Fart' Explains Why a Zombie Star Keeps Flashing Earth
summary:
A very strange pair of stars keeps flashing Earth with X-ray bursts. Now scientists understand why: an enormous cosmic 'fart' is causing a zombie star to flare up repeatedly.

About 13,000 light-years away lies a binary system called BP Crucis. It contains a blue hypergiant star, Wray 977, roughly 60 times larger than the Sun, and a neutron star named GX 301-2. A neutron star is the ultradense leftover of a star that exploded. GX 301-2 packs the Sun's mass into an object only about 12 miles across. It's a pulsar — a rapidly spinning neutron star with a powerful magnetic field that shoots out beams of X-rays. Every 11 minutes, one beam sweeps past Earth, and telescopes detect a flash.

But GX 301-2 also emits extra X-ray flares. Until now, no one knew why. In a new study published Sept. 18 in Science Advances, researchers used the XRISM space telescope — a joint mission of NASA and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency — to observe the system. They found that the neutron star flares every time it passes through a giant plume of stellar wind — a stream of charged particles — shooting from Wray 977 at 335,000 mph.

GX 301-2 circles Wray 977 every 41.5 days, flaring when it reaches its closest and farthest points from its partner, with the strongest flares at its closest point. During a 16-hour observation, XRISM captured detailed X-ray spectra showing how the plume ebbed and flowed around the neutron star.

"We've never before seen clear indications of wind plasma falling onto a compact object," said lead author Roi Rahin, a researcher at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center. When enough gas piles onto the neutron star's surface, it erupts in bright X-rays.

The discovery opens the door to studying similar systems. "The BP Crucis system is an ideal laboratory," said NASA's Brian Williams. Next, scientists hope to observe more flares to understand this cosmic odd couple.
why_it_matters: Neutron stars are natural laboratories for physics that cannot be recreated on Earth, so explaining how they feed and flare sharpens models of matter under extreme gravity and magnetism. It also matters for astronomy itself: almost everything known about such objects comes from light caught by space telescopes, so a better theory of these flares improves how scientists read signals from thousands of similar systems.

background_read: A neutron star is what is left after a massive star runs out of fuel and explodes as a supernova: the core collapses until protons and electrons crush together into neutrons. The result packs more mass than the Sun into a ball only a few miles wide, making it one of the densest objects known.

Pulsars, a type of neutron star, were first detected by radio astronomers who noticed clock-like pulses arriving at very regular intervals; the graduate student Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted the earliest signals, and the discovery forced physicists to take these strange objects seriously. Because they spin so steadily, pulsars are used as cosmic clocks.

When a neutron star has a normal companion star, the pair is called an X-ray binary: the compact object's gravity pulls gas off the companion, and that gas heats up and glows in X-rays before falling in. Studying that flow is a key way to test how matter behaves under extreme gravity.

XRISM is the X-ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission, a space telescope built jointly by NASA and JAXA (the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, Japan's equivalent of NASA). X-ray astronomy has to be done from space because Earth's atmosphere blocks X-rays before they reach the ground. The results were published in Science Advances, a peer-reviewed journal.

perspectives.description: For the researchers, the result is a clean explanation: flares line up with the neutron star's passage through its companion's wind, and the timing matches the orbit. It also demonstrates that XRISM can capture gas flows in fine detail, which is exactly what the mission was built to do. Astronomers gain a template for interpreting other X-ray binaries.

The evidence rests on a single 16-hour observation of one binary, and while the wind explanation fits the timing, other contributions such as clumps of gas or magnetic effects are hard to rule out. The authors themselves call for more flares to be observed. Until repeated measurements confirm the pattern, the conclusion remains a strong hypothesis rather than a certainty.

Astronomers have long used binary systems as laboratories because a compact object and a normal star interact in ways a lone star cannot. Mass transfer between the two drives X-ray emission, and comparing many such systems reveals how stars evolve and how much material they lose through winds. This result adds a well-observed example to that growing catalogue.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — a laboratory for extreme physics
perspectives.description: The next step is watching more flares to see whether the wind plume changes over time and whether similar patterns appear in other pulsar binaries. Better models of accreting neutron stars could also refine measurements of their mass and radius, which constrain how matter behaves at nuclear densities. Ongoing and future X-ray missions will make such long-term monitoring possible.
